#!/usr/bin/env bash
# One-shot per-boot health check of every custom guard on this live session.
#
# Every live session is a fresh boot with no persistence — you cannot assume
# yesterday's setup carried over, and a crashed COSMIC shell (2026-08-23) can
# leave user units in surprising states. This runs ~2 min after login via
# guards-doctor.timer and answers, in one notification: are the guards armed,
# are the resources sane, are the CLIs still authed. Also runnable by hand
# anytime as `guards-doctor.sh`.
#
# Every external call is timeout-wrapped — a hung network or a wedged disk
# must never hang the doctor.
set -uo pipefail

STATE_DIR="$HOME/.local/state/guards-doctor"
LOG_FILE="$STATE_DIR/doctor.log"
mkdir -p "$STATE_DIR"
log() { echo "$(date -Iseconds) $*" >> "$LOG_FILE"; }

NOTIFY=0
[ "${1:-}" = "--notify" ] && NOTIFY=1

PASS=0; FAIL=0; WARN=0
ok()   { PASS=$((PASS+1)); printf '  ✓ %s\n' "$1"; }
bad()  { FAIL=$((FAIL+1)); printf '  ✗ %s\n' "$1"; }
warn() { WARN=$((WARN+1)); printf '  ⚠ %s\n' "$1"; }

THRESHOLD=75  # keep in sync with disk-cleanup.sh

echo "=== guards doctor $(date -Iseconds) ==="

# ---- guard units -----------------------------------------------------------
if systemctl --user is-active --quiet disk-cleanup.timer; then
  ok "disk-cleanup.timer active (5-min storage guard)"
else
  bad "disk-cleanup.timer NOT active — start: systemctl --user enable --now disk-cleanup.timer"
fi

if systemctl --user is-active --quiet battery-guard.service; then
  ok "battery-guard.service running"
else
  bad "battery-guard.service NOT running — start: systemctl --user start battery-guard.service"
fi

lid_state="OFF (lid close suspends normally)"
systemctl --user is-active --quiet lid-guard.service && lid_state="ON (lid close does nothing)"
printf '  • lid-guard: %s\n' "$lid_state"

if systemctl --user is-enabled --quiet guards-doctor.timer 2>/dev/null; then
  ok "guards-doctor.timer enabled (this check re-runs each boot)"
else
  warn "guards-doctor.timer not enabled"
fi

# ---- resources -------------------------------------------------------------
pct="$(df --output=pcent / | tail -1 | tr -dc '0-9')"
avail_mb=$(( $(df --output=avail / | tail -1 | tr -dc '0-9') / 1024 ))
if [ "${pct:-100}" -lt "$THRESHOLD" ]; then
  ok "disk ${pct}% used (${avail_mb}MB free, threshold ${THRESHOLD}%)"
else
  bad "disk ${pct}% used ≥ threshold ${THRESHOLD}% (${avail_mb}MB free)"
fi

mem_avail_mb=$(( $(free -k | awk '/^Mem:/{print $7}') / 1024 ))
swap_pct=$(free -k | awk '/^Swap:/{if ($2>0) print int($3*100/$2); else print 0}')
if [ "$mem_avail_mb" -ge 1500 ] && [ "${swap_pct:-0}" -lt 40 ]; then
  ok "RAM ${mem_avail_mb}MB available, swap ${swap_pct}% used"
else
  warn "RAM pressure: ${mem_avail_mb}MB available, swap ${swap_pct}% used (/tmp is RAM-backed)"
fi

printf '  • /tmp (RAM tmpfs): %s used\n' "$(du -sh /tmp 2>/dev/null | cut -f1)"

# ---- battery ---------------------------------------------------------------
bat="$(cat /sys/class/power_supply/BAT0/capacity 2>/dev/null || echo '?')"
ac="$(cat /sys/class/power_supply/AC/online 2>/dev/null || echo '?')"
if [ "$ac" = "1" ]; then
  printf '  • battery: %s%% (on AC)\n' "$bat"
elif [ "${bat:-100}" -gt 30 ]; then
  printf '  • battery: %s%% (on battery, above alarm tier)\n' "$bat"
else
  warn "battery ${bat}% on battery — guard should be alarming"
fi

# ---- CLI auth (network calls, hard-timeboxed) ------------------------------
# A flaky network must read as "unknown/offline", never as "logged out" —
# otherwise the doctor cries wolf every time DNS hiccups.
if timeout 6 curl -sfI https://api.github.com >/dev/null 2>&1 \
   || timeout 6 getent hosts api.github.com >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  online=1
else
  online=0
  warn "network unreachable — CLI auth checks skipped (not a logout)"
fi

if [ "$online" -eq 1 ]; then
  # One retry each: transient DNS blips (observed live) must not read as logout.
  retry() { # retry <timeout> <cmd...> — runs cmd twice, returns first success
    local t="$1"; shift
    timeout "$t" "$@" >/dev/null 2>&1 && return 0
    sleep 2
    timeout "$t" "$@" >/dev/null 2>&1
  }

  if retry 15 gh auth status; then
    ok "gh authenticated ($(timeout 15 gh api user --jq .login 2>/dev/null || echo '?'))"
  else
    bad "gh NOT authenticated — run: gh auth login"
  fi

  # vercel is a slow-starting Node CLI: measured 8.6–14s+ depending on network,
  # so a generous ceiling plus the shared retry
  vc_user="$(timeout 40 vercel whoami 2>/dev/null | tail -1)"
  [ -z "$vc_user" ] && { sleep 2; vc_user="$(timeout 40 vercel whoami 2>/dev/null | tail -1)"; }
  if [ -n "$vc_user" ]; then
    ok "vercel authenticated ($vc_user)"
  else
    bad "vercel NOT authenticated — run: vercel login"
  fi

  ts_user="$(timeout 15 turso auth whoami 2>/dev/null || timeout 15 turso whoami 2>/dev/null | tail -1)"
  [ -z "$ts_user" ] && { sleep 2; ts_user="$(timeout 15 turso auth whoami 2>/dev/null || timeout 15 turso whoami 2>/dev/null | tail -1)"; }
  if [ -n "$ts_user" ]; then
    ok "turso authenticated ($ts_user)"
  else
    bad "turso NOT authenticated — run: turso auth login"
  fi
fi

# ---- internal SSD watch (informational) ------------------------------------
# Why live-boot at all: the internal SSD's SATA link drops at 6.0 Gbps
# (healthy per SMART; marginal physical connection). Track its state and any
# link errors this boot so degradation is visible early.
sda_sz="$(lsblk -ndo SIZE /dev/sda 2>/dev/null || true)"
if [ -n "$sda_sz" ]; then
  printf '  • internal SSD (sda): present (%s)\n' "$sda_sz"
else
  printf '  • internal SSD (sda): absent/disabled this boot\n'
fi
ata_errs="$(journalctl -k -b --no-pager 2>/dev/null | grep -cE 'DID_BAD_TARGET|ata[0-9]+: (hardreset failed|link is slow)' || true)"
if [ "${ata_errs:-0}" -eq 0 ]; then
  printf '  • SATA link errors this boot: none seen\n'
else
  warn "SATA link errors this boot: $ata_errs (see journalctl -k -b | grep ata)"
fi

# ---- summary ----------------------------------------------------------------
summary_line="${PASS} ok, ${FAIL} failed, ${WARN} warned"
echo "=== ${summary_line} ==="
log "${summary_line}"

if [ "$NOTIFY" -eq 1 ]; then
  if [ "$FAIL" -eq 0 ]; then
    urgency="normal"; icon="emblem-ok"; head="Guards armed — all checks passed"
    [ "$WARN" -gt 0 ] && head="Guards armed (${WARN} warning${WARN:+s})"
  else
    urgency="critical"; icon="dialog-error"; head="⚠ Guards: ${FAIL} check(s) FAILED"
  fi
  ac_note="(on AC)"
  [ "$ac" != "1" ] && ac_note="(on battery)"
  command -v notify-send >/dev/null 2>&1 && \
    notify-send -u "$urgency" -i "$icon" "$head" \
      "Disk ${pct}% · RAM ${mem_avail_mb}MB avail · battery ${bat}% ${ac_note}
gh/vercel/turso: see terminal — full detail: guards-doctor.sh" 2>/dev/null
fi

# nonzero exit only for real failures so timers/logs stay quiet otherwise
[ "$FAIL" -eq 0 ]

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Hourly reminder-only sweep for uncommitted work.
#
# On an ephemeral live session the one unrecoverable loss is uncommitted work
# when the session dies (it has happened). This never commits, pushes, or
# touches anything — it only notices dirty repos and pings, at most once every
# NUDGE_INTERVAL_SECS per repo, until you commit or stash.
set -uo pipefail

STATE_DIR="$HOME/.local/state/dirty-work-nudge"
LAST_NOTIFY="$STATE_DIR/notified.tsv"     # repo<TAB>epoch_of_last_nudge
LOG_FILE="$STATE_DIR/nudge.log"
NUDGE_INTERVAL_SECS=$(( 2 * 60 * 60 ))    # per-repo re-nudge cadence
DIRTY_MIN_AGE_SECS=$(( 45 * 60 ))         # ignore just-edited work-in-flight
mkdir -p "$STATE_DIR"

log() { echo "$(date -Iseconds) $*" >> "$LOG_FILE"; }
now=$(date +%s)

notify() {
  command -v notify-send >/dev/null 2>&1 && \
    notify-send -u normal -i git "$1" "$2" 2>/dev/null
  return 0
}

# Repo discovery: default roots scanned to depth 4, heavy/never-touch trees
# pruned. Extra roots (one path per line) in ~/.config/guards/project-dirs.
mapfile -t roots < <(
  { cat ~/.config/guards/project-dirs 2>/dev/null || true
    echo "$HOME"
  } | sed "s|^~|$HOME|" | grep -v '^$' | sort -u
)

prune_expr=( \( -name node_modules -o -name .cache -o -name .hermes \
               -o -name .cargo -o -name .rustup -o -name .npm \
               -o -name .local -o -name .config -o -name snap \
               -o -name .claude -o -name .turso \) -prune )

repos=()
for root in "${roots[@]}"; do
  [ -d "$root" ] || continue
  while IFS= read -r g; do
    repos+=( "${g%/.git}" )
  done < <(timeout 60 find "$root" "${prune_expr[@]}" -o \
             -maxdepth 4 -type d -name .git -print 2>/dev/null)
done

declare -A seen=()
dirty_count=0
for repo in "${repos[@]}"; do
  [ -d "$repo/.git" ] || continue
  [ -n "${seen[$repo]:-}" ] && continue
  seen["$repo"]=1

  changes="$(timeout 15 git -C "$repo" status --porcelain 2>/dev/null)" || continue
  [ -n "$changes" ] || continue
  n=$(printf '%s\n' "$changes" | wc -l)

  # Skip brand-new edits: mtime of the newest uncommitted path within window
  newest=0
  while IFS= read -r f; do
    [ -n "$f" ] || continue
    f="${f#??? }"
    f="$(printf '%s' "$f" | sed -e 's/^"//' -e 's/"$//' -e 's/.* -> //')"
    [ -e "$repo/$f" ] || continue
    m=$(stat -c%Y "$repo/$f" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
    [ "$m" -gt "$newest" ] && newest=$m
  done <<< "$changes"
  [ $(( now - newest )) -ge "$DIRTY_MIN_AGE_SECS" ] || continue

  branch="$(timeout 10 git -C "$repo" rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo '?')"
  last=0
  if [ -f "$LAST_NOTIFY" ]; then
    last=$(awk -F'\t' -v r="$repo" '$1==r{print $2}' "$LAST_NOTIFY")
  fi
  [ $(( now - ${last:-0} )) -ge "$NUDGE_INTERVAL_SECS" ] || continue

  notify "Uncommitted work: $(basename "$repo")" \
    "$n changed file(s) on branch '${branch}'.
Reminder only — nothing is committed or pushed automatically."
  log "nudged: $repo ($n files, branch $branch)"
  printf '%s\t%s\n' "$repo" "$now" >> "$STATE_DIR/.notified.tmp"
  dirty_count=$((dirty_count+1))
done

# merge this round's nudges into the state file, pruning stale entries (>48h)
if [ -f "$STATE_DIR/.notified.tmp" ]; then
  cat "$LAST_NOTIFY" "$STATE_DIR/.notified.tmp" 2>/dev/null | \
    awk -F'\t' -v cutoff=$(( now - 172800 )) '$2 > cutoff' | sort -u -k1,1 > "$LAST_NOTIFY.new"
  mv "$LAST_NOTIFY.new" "$LAST_NOTIFY"
  rm -f "$STATE_DIR/.notified.tmp"
fi

log "scan done: ${#seen[@]} repos checked, $dirty_count nudged"

[Unit]
Description=Run guards-doctor once per boot, ~2 min after login

[Timer]
OnBootSec=2min
AccuracySec=15s

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

[Unit]
Description=Nudge about uncommitted work hourly (reminder only)

[Timer]
OnBootSec=25min
OnUnitActiveSec=1h
AccuracySec=1min

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

7	---
8	
9	## What this place is
10	
11	The Inner Circle is a home for people doing meaningful work while it is still becoming.
12	
13	"Meaningful work" is not limited to software or startups. It includes any intentional act of creation — building a product, writing, research, teaching, craft, raising a family with intention, building a community, changing careers, creating art, starting a small business.
14	
15	The domain can change. The stage does not. We care about the long, mostly invisible stretch before recognition.
16	
17	## What this place is not
18	
19	Not a hustle-culture community. Not a productivity brand. Not startup theater. Not a place that manufactures status. Not a social network. Not a membership product with dashboards and profiles. Not motivational. Not inspirational-quote culture.
20	
21	We do not promise transformation. We offer recognition.
22	
23	## The anti-persona
24	
25	This is not for people looking for shortcuts, status, or performance. It is for people who find satisfaction in the act of making something meaningful — even when almost no one is watching.
26	
27	If recognition comes later, it is welcomed. It is never the reason the work exists.
28	
29	## How we write
30	
31	Observations over advice. Documentation over performance. Questions over certainty. Specificity over generality. Honesty over polish.
32	
33	Never write like marketing. Never create urgency or scarcity. Never promise transformation. Never manufacture authority. If a sentence could appear on ten other websites, delete it.
34	
35	## The north star
36	
37	Every decision — design, writing, feature, or future direction — is measured against one idea:
38	
39	Most people only notice things after they succeed. We are interested in everything that happens before that.
40

Most people only notice things after they succeed.

We are interested in everything that happens before that.

This is not a slogan. It is the filter for every decision made here.

---

## What this place is

The Inner Circle is a home for people doing meaningful work while it is still becoming.

"Meaningful work" is not limited to software or startups. It includes any intentional act of creation — building a product, writing, research, teaching, craft, raising a family with intention, building a community, changing careers, creating art, starting a small business.

The domain can change. The stage does not. We care about the long, mostly invisible stretch before recognition.

## What this place is not

Not a hustle-culture community. Not a productivity brand. Not startup theater. Not a place that manufactures status. Not a social network. Not a membership product with dashboards and profiles. Not motivational. Not inspirational-quote culture.

We do not promise transformation. We offer recognition.

## The anti-persona

This is not for people looking for shortcuts, status, or performance. It is for people who find satisfaction in the act of making something meaningful — even when almost no one is watching.

If recognition comes later, it is welcomed. It is never the reason the work exists.

## How we write

Observations over advice. Documentation over performance. Questions over certainty. Specificity over generality. Honesty over polish.

Never write like marketing. Never create urgency or scarcity. Never promise transformation. Never manufacture authority. If a sentence could appear on ten other websites, delete it.

## The north star

Every decision — design, writing, feature, or future direction — is measured against one idea:

Most people only notice things after they succeed. We are interested in everything that happens before that.

If it does not serve this idea, remove it.

file.content:
# The Inner Circle

A quiet, editorial home for the meaningful work that happens before anyone notices.

Built with Next.js (App Router), Tailwind CSS, MDX content, and barely-there motion.
Deployed on Vercel.

## Local development

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

## Content

- `content/manifesto.mdx` — the timeless document
- `content/journal/*.mdx` — notebook entries
- `content/work/*.mdx` — living work, shown honestly
- `content/now/now.mdx` — quiet status page

## Principles

Observations over advice. Documentation over performance. Questions over
certainty. Specificity over generality. Honesty over polish.

The website may evolve. The Constitution does not.

I've now read every source file in the repo. Complete picture of the codebase:

**The repo truth (as of commit f6792a2, 2026-07-31):**
- Next.js 14 App Router, Tailwind 3, framer-motion (FadeIn only), next-mdx-remote for MDX
- 7 routes: / (essay-home), /manifesto, /journal (+[slug]), /work (+[slug]), /now, /join
- Content: manifesto.mdx, 2 journal entries, 1 work entry ("This website"), now.mdx
- Design: warm paper #f4f1ea, ink #14130f, accent #8a6f4e (bronze/ochre — NOT the gold #C8A96E from portfolio doc; that was the old portfolio), Newsreader serif + Inter
- Join = WhatsApp link only (https://chat.whatsapp.com/GRsVbQi7WlzEm4M4wf4YXB)

1. The site is philosophically faithful to brief #1 (the "before recognition" philosophy) — homepage is an essay, restrained palette, reading-first.

That preserves its context (whatever it has) and redirects.

Actually cleaner: stop it and relaunch properly? SendMessage continues it with context intact — fine since its context is nearly empty anyway. Let me send a comprehensive mission message.

Also meanwhile, I can fetch the live TIC site myself right now via WebFetch (quick check for drift) — that was my other parallel intent.

So now:

Then while agent works, I'll do my own direct pass on jaligroup.org too? The user asked me personally to look in depth. The agent dossier plus my own reads of key pages would be ideal. src = open('jali-bundle.js', encoding='utf-8', errors='replace').read()

seen=set(); out=[]

    seen.add(t)
    if re.search(r'[a-z] [a-z]', t) and not re.match(r'^[#\{\[\(<%]', t) and 'function' not in t and 'webkit' not in t:
        out.append(t)
print(f"== {len(out)} CONTENT STRINGS (in bundle order) ==\n")
for s in out: print(s + '\n')
EOF

import re, html
src = open('jali-bundle.js', encoding='utf-8', errors='replace').read()
strings = re.findall(r'"((?:[^"\\]|\\.){25,800})"', src)

seen=set(); out=[]
for s in strings:
    t = s.encode().decode('unicode_escape', errors='replace').strip()
    t = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', t)
    if t in seen or len(t) < 30: continue
    if bad.search(t): continue
    words = t.split(' ')
    letters = sum(c.isalpha() or c in ' ,.\'\-!?;:%&()’‘“”—…/' for c in t)
    if len(words) < 5 or letters/len(t) < 0.85: continue
    seen.add(t); out.append(t)
print(f"== {len(out)} HUMAN-READABLE STRINGS ==\n")
for s in out: print("•", s)
EOF

  • The Jali content and strategy engine behind you
    • For Entrepreneurs & Investors

    We Match You With The Creator Who Changes Everything

    Your business works. What it needs is distribution and trust, and those cannot be bought with ad spend. We match you with the creator whose audience is your customer base, structure the equity partnership, and manage the relationship so the flywheel actually turns.

      Mainly non-tech. We back real-world businesses with products people touch, taste, wear, visit, and live with, because that is where creator trust converts hardest.

      Creators ready to convert trust into equity. Entrepreneurs and investors ready to grow with distribution money can't buy. Both boards are by waitlist.

      We are building it. It is called the Jali Tribe, and it sits inside a group that owns media and takes equity in the people it serves. This page is what we are building, why it works, and what we are still missing.

      Everything we build comes from one observation. The creator and the entrepreneur are each holding the missing half of the other person's business, and the whole market has been built to keep them apart.

      The creator

      All attention. No business.

      Two hundred thousand followers and no asset. Making other people's brands famous for a fee that lands ninety days late. Brilliant at the part that is hardest to teach, and completely unserved on the part that decides whether any of it lasts.

      The advice never changes. Post more. Be consistent. Build your personal brand. All true, all useless alone, because none of it answers the only question that matters, which is what exactly are you building that keeps paying you when you stop posting.

      What we give them: revenue, structure, ownership, a real business underneath the audience.
      The entrepreneur

      All business. No attention.

      A real company, real margins, real staff, and almost nobody knows it exists. Burning money on ads that stop working the day the budget stops. Watching people with a tenth of the substance take the market on distribution alone.

      They are told to hire an agency, run more paid media, do more SEO. Nobody tells them the truth, which is that in this decade the company with the story and the face wins, and the one without it pays for every single customer forever.

      What we give them: visibility, distribution, digital growth, a story people actually repeat.
    One has the audience the other needs. One has the business the other needs. We are building the room where that trade finally happens.
    Premise 02

    The correct trade is equity on both sides of the table.

    A creator who takes a piece of a company in exchange for eighteen months of distribution has done a better deal than one who takes a fee. The entrepreneur who gives it up has bought growth he could not have bought with cash. We call this the Angel-Creator model. We teach it, we broker it, and we do it ourselves.

    Premise 03

    Nobody scales alone, so the room is the product.

    Every serious business generation in history came out of a room. Talent clusters or it dissipates. We are building the cluster deliberately instead of hoping it happens by accident, and we are putting both sides of the trade inside it.

    Most companies here pick one. A community, or a media brand, or a fund. Each is a weak business alone. Together they are close to unbeatable, because each arm makes the other two cheaper to run and harder to copy.

    Arm one

    Tribe

    The room itself. A paid membership for creators and entrepreneurs who are already past the beginning and stuck before the next level.

    Creators come in to build a business under the audience. Entrepreneurs come in to build an audience over the business. They train together, and then they trade with each other.

    Arm two

    Media

    Our own audience, permanently. A podcast, a slate of shows, and a pitch programme where founders make their case on camera.

    Media is how the Tribe fills itself without paying for a click. It is also a service we deliver to members, because a business featured on our channels gets the one thing money buys badly, which is attention that is already earned.

    Arm three

    Capital

    We take equity in creator and founder businesses and pay for it with distribution, operating support, and the room.

    Not passive money. The kind of ownership where our involvement is the reason the company works. The Tribe finds them, Media makes them, Capital owns a piece of what they become.

    We are not selling a course to people who want to be creators. We are building the institution that the best creators and the best founders will run their businesses from.

    The credibility matters for one reason. In this market almost everyone teaching is teaching from a position they have never personally held. We are building the thing we describe while we describe it, and every member watches us do it.

    It is also the internal standard. We do not announce what we have not built, and we do not sell what we have not survived. It is slower, and it is the only reason people stay.

    Not a community with a chat group. A membership with physical infrastructure and real economics attached, serving both sides of the room.

    Infrastructure

    A studio in every city we sit in

    Partnered content studios so any member can walk in and shoot for free or close to it. Eventually we own them. First we partner into them, which is faster and costs almost nothing.

    Economics

    The Tribe Partner Program

    Members become partners. When they bring people into the room, they earn. The membership stops being something people buy and becomes something they build with us.

    Distribution

    Member collaborations on our channels

    Members collaborate on Jali content and borrow the audience we already built. A person joins with fifteen thousand followers and leaves a campaign with visibility they could not have bought.

    Revenue

    Brand deals routed through the room

    We bring brands in and place real paid work with members. A membership that returns itself in one collaboration stops being a cost and becomes the most profitable line in a member's year.

    The room, physically

    Gatherings in the best venues in the world

    Dinners, hangouts, private rooms, rooftops, hotels. Partnered rather than paid for. When a member walks into a Jali table in their city, the room itself tells them what they joined.

    The engine

    Shows that make members famous

    The podcast and the pitch show put member businesses in front of an audience that buys. Media stops being marketing and becomes a service delivered to the people inside the room.

    Year 1

    The room becomes undeniable

    Studios signed in the first three cities. Venues wherever members cluster. The Partner Program running. First brand collaborations paid out. The Tribe stops being a membership people describe and becomes one they show.

    Year 2

    Media carries its own weight

    Sponsored shows, a pitch programme with real capital behind it, and a media arm that is profitable rather than promotional. Members get known for their businesses. The Tribe fills itself.

    Year 3

    Capital starts compounding

    A portfolio of businesses we own pieces of, built by creators and founders who met each other in our room. The year this stops looking like a community business and starts looking like a holding company.

    Year 5

    The default answer

    A creator or a founder anywhere in the world crosses six figures and asks one question, which is where do I go next. There is one answer, and it is not a platform, a course or a conference. It is a room, and we built it.

    This is not you if

    You need the map drawn first

    • You need an established brand behind you before anyone takes your call.
    • You want a defined process on day one. We are writing the process and you are holding the pen.
    • You measure your work in meetings attended rather than agreements signed.
    • You are uncomfortable with public accountability. We build in front of people here, including when it goes badly.
    • You want to be busy. We need you to be effective, and those are different jobs.

The Story

A name that describes what already was

In October 2025, a WhatsApp group opened in Kenya under a name that made perfect sense at the time:{" "} Ken Builds. Most of what happened inside it revolved around things Kennedy was building — software, experiments, ideas at various stages of almost working. People gathered because of that work, and for a while the name told the whole truth.

Then something became clear, slowly the way obvious things do: the interesting part was never one person’s output. It was the people around it. Different disciplines, different towns, different seasons of life — students, founders, parents, engineers, people who would never call themselves builders but who were quietly making things anyway.

The name started feeling too small.

So it changed — announced to the group not as a launch, but as an observation. One line from that message survived every draft:

Because I finally found a name that describes what already was.

That is the whole origin. No pivot deck, no strategy offsite. A room of people noticed what it had become, and went looking for language honest enough to hold it.

The circle is still small enough that everyone in it knows this story personally. It will not stay that way, and it should not — but the origin is worth keeping exactly where it can be found.

This site is part of the same honesty. It documents itself while unfinished, keeps its promises in public, and says where it is from.

{SITE.place}

); }

input.content:
Most communities organize around a category — AI, startups, design, fitness, faith, money. This one is organized around a moment in time: the long stretch when meaningful work exists but nobody has noticed yet.

That choice has consequences. Here is the thinking, written down while it is still being tested.

## Premise one — the stage is the point

What someone is building matters less than when they are building it. A student writing her first curriculum and a founder shipping his first product are standing in the same place, even if their fields never touch. The domain can change. The stage does not.

## Premise two — recognition, not transformation

We do not promise to make anyone better, richer, faster, or more disciplined. That promise is everywhere already, and it is mostly noise. What this place offers is smaller and rarer: the experience of being seen doing serious work before it has an audience — and discovering you are not the only one living there.

## Premise three — witnesses make beginnings real

A beginning kept entirely private is easy to abandon; no one knows it existed. A beginning seen by even one other person becomes harder to walk away from. The circle exists to be that witness. Not an audience — witnesses. The difference is that an audience watches you perform, and a witness can testify that you were there.

## What exists today

Three things, honestly named:

- **The circle** — a WhatsApp room, small and intentional, where people share what they are actually working on. It is the living heart of this.
- **This site** — the public record. A manifesto that rarely changes, a journal that accumulates, and work documented while unfinished.
- **A founder** — Kennedy, who started the room and writes most of what is here, for now.

## What comes next

Held loosely. None of this is a promise with a date attached.

**First, the record accumulates.** More journal entries. More work shown before it is finished — and not only the founder's. The measure of health is when someone else's beginning appears here.

**Then, the room begins to belong to its members.** A rhythm that runs without one person pushing it. A table in Nairobi before a stage anywhere. Names on this site that we did not put there ourselves.

**Eventually, beyond Kenya.** The stage we organize around is universal; the place we are from is specific. Both are kept.

## What we are still missing

Said plainly, because pretending otherwise would break everything above:

- The site still mostly documents one person's beginnings. That is the honest state of a young circle, and it is the first thing to change.
- The rhythm of the room still depends on Kennedy showing up. Culture should outlive its founder's attention.
- There is no proof yet that a stranger can arrive, recognize themselves, and find their place here without being personally invited. That proof is the whole test.

If a day comes when those three sentences are no longer true, this page will say so.

import { FadeIn } from "@/components/FadeIn"; import { TeaserLink } from "@/components/TeaserLink"; export default function HomePage() { return (

A quiet place to be recognized

Most people only notice a thing after it has succeeded — after the launch, the funding, the headlines. We are interested in everything that happens before that.

The uncertainty. The notebook full of crossed-out ideas. The prototypes that never ship. The late nights. The conversations that never become posts. The quiet work that happens while nobody is watching.

The Inner Circle is a home for that stage of work. Not a community portal. Not a landing page designed to convert. A place where the right person recognizes themselves — and feels, perhaps for the first time, that they are not alone in working this way.

---
title: "Restraint is a design decision, not an absence"
date: "2026-08-23"
summary: "The promised second piece: why every feature this site refuses is part of the architecture."
---

Every website is built twice — once by what gets added, and once by what gets refused. The second build takes longer.

When this site was being shaped, the list of things it could have had was long and reasonable: a testimonials wall, a members counter ticking upward, a newsletter popup with a discount for early joiners, animated statistics, a progress bar that follows you down the page. Every item on that list works. That is exactly the problem. Things that work on everyone are invisible on anyone.

Restraint gets described as minimalism, which makes it sound like an aesthetic preference — clean lines, generous margins. But the actual discipline is closer to hospitality. A crowded room tells the visitor to hurry up and consume. A quiet one says: nothing here needs you, so anything you give is real attention, freely spent.

There is also a harder reason. This place claims to care about work done without applause. A site that applauds itself constantly would be making the claim false in the same breath it was making it.

So the rule going forward stays unfriendly to growth hacks: if a feature exists mainly to make this place look more alive than it is, it does not go in. Even when — especially when — it would work.

---
title: "Ordinary rooms"
date: "2026-08-23"
summary: "Most serious work happens in rooms that would make a terrible photograph — and that is exactly the point."
---

Almost nothing worth building gets built in the rooms that photograph well.

The real ones have a fan doing most of the climate control. A desk that came with the house. The neighbor's radio going through its afternoon routine somewhere behind the wall. In Ruiru, in Thika, in a thousand towns that never appear in startup photography, people are deep into the unglamorous middle of things — the fourth rewrite, the third rejection, the version nobody has seen.

There is a particular loneliness to it that no one photographs either. Not dramatic loneliness. The ordinary kind, where you have been talking to yourself about a project for so long that your own voice starts sounding like speculation.

That is the room this circle is for. Not the rooftop with the skyline — anyone can be interesting up there. The test of a place like this is whether it means anything on a Tuesday afternoon in an ordinary room, when the work is neither finished nor failing, just unfinished, and the only reason to keep going is that someone might want the thing to exist.

We think they will. That is the whole bet.

---
title: "The circle, itself"
date: "2026-08-23"
state: "In progress"
summary: "The hardest thing being built here is not software. A room is a product you cannot screenshot."
---

Of everything being worked on in and around this site, the most difficult object has no repository: the circle itself.

A community looks simple from outside — people, a chat, some rituals. From inside it behaves more like an organism with exactly one fragile organ: attention. Rooms do not die from arguments. They die from silence that nobody noticed, from weeks where the founder was busy and no one wanted to be the first to speak into a quiet space.

What has been learned so far, honestly:

- Renaming the room (from Ken Builds) changed how people saw it faster than any feature could have. Language ships.
- Rituals beat enthusiasm. The gentle weekly rhythm does more than motivation ever did, because it survives bad weeks.
- The founder's presence is both the engine and the bottleneck. Everything currently depends on one person showing up. That is the known weakness.

What comes next: letting other people's beginnings appear on this site. The measure of whether this work is succeeding is embarrassingly concrete — when someone who is not Kennedy documents their unfinished thing here, version 1.0 ships.

# The Inner Circle

A quiet, editorial home for the meaningful work that happens before anyone notices.

Built with Next.js (App Router), Tailwind CSS, MDX content, and barely-there motion.
Deployed on Vercel.

## Local development

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

## Structure

- `/story` — where the name came from (origin + founder)
- `content/manifesto.mdx` — the timeless document
- `content/vision.mdx` → `/vision` — what this is becoming, honestly
- `content/journal/*.mdx` — notebook entries, accumulated not scheduled
- `content/work/*.mdx` — living work, shown while unfinished
- `content/now/now.mdx` — quiet status page
- `/join` — the one intentional step into the circle

Infrastructure: sitemap (`app/sitemap.ts`), robots, RSS feed (`app/rss.xml`),
generated Open Graph image (`app/opengraph-image.tsx`). Shared constants in
`lib/site.ts`.

## Principles

Observations over advice. Documentation over performance. Questions over
certainty. Specificity over generality. Honesty over polish.

The website may evolve. The Constitution does not.

content.content:
# Tally API — Extracted Details

## 1) Authentication
- Header format: every request requires an `"Authorization: Bearer <token>"` header.
- Base URL: `"https://api.tally.so"`
- Token source: the docs link to developers.tally.so/api-reference/api-keys ("Get your API key here"); the FAQ adds that you'll "Find your API key in your account settings."

## 2) Create a form — endpoint & payload
Endpoint: `POST /forms`. Exact curl lines as written (split to respect length limits):

```
curl --request POST \
   --url https://api.tally.so/forms \
   --header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' \
   --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
```

Payload fragments, verbatim:
```
'{ "status": "PUBLISHED", "blocks": [
{ "uuid": "<title-block-uuid>", "type": "FORM_TITLE",
"payload": { "title": "Client Intake – Acme Co" } },
...copied from GET /forms/{formId} ] }'
```

Structural rules stated on the page:
- "`status` is required ('PUBLISHED', or 'DRAFT'/blank for a draft)."
- There's no `name` field — "the API ignores it"; the name comes from the first block, "which must be a FORM_TITLE block."
- Dropdowns use separate option blocks: `"type": "DROPDOWN_OPTION"` sharing a `"groupUuid"` with the parent dropdown.
- ⚠️ Not on this page: a complete catalog of supported field types, labels/options schemas, or any `required` flag. It defers to the "Block Schema Reference" at developers.tally.so/blocks-reference/dropdown-option.

## 3) Create-response shape
Not documented on this page. No sample response showing where the form id or URL lives is included.

## 4) Retrieve submissions
Exact lines:
```
curl --request GET \
   --url https://api.tally.so/forms/{formId}/submissions \
   --header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
```
Pagination: pass `"page"` and `"limit"` params; check the `"hasMore"` boolean (alongside page, limit, total). Deletion via `DELETE .../submissions/{submissionId}` "Returns `204` on success," moving items to Trash with a recovery window. Webhooks are recommended over polling given the "100 requests/minute" rate limit.

## 5) Embed / public URL patterns
Not covered anywhere in this page's content.

# Creating a Form via the Tally API

**Note:** This page only documents `FORM_TITLE`. It contains no examples of `LABEL`, `INPUT_TEXT`, `TEXTAREA`, `MULTIPLE_CHOICE_OPTION`, or checkbox blocks — you'd need the full docs index at developers.tally.so/llms.txt for those.

## Prerequisites
- A Tally account
- An API key

## Request

The guide instructs you to "send a POST request to the `/forms` endpoint" at `https://api.tally.so/forms`, with these headers:
- `Authorization: Bearer <token>`
- `Content-Type: application/json`

### Payload structure

The body is JSON containing two top-level keys:

1. **`status`** — set to `"PUBLISHED"`
2. **`blocks`** — an array of block objects

Each block object shown uses these fields:

| Field | Example value |
|---|---|
| `uuid` | `"6ef8675d-33cb-419b-a81e-93982e726f2e"` |
| `type` | `"FORM_TITLE"` |
| `groupUuid` | `"073c835f-7ad4-459c-866d-4108b6b7e2e1"` |
| `groupType` | `"TEXT"` |
| `payload.title` | `"Test"` |
| `payload.html` | `"Test"` |

So the minimal working body is essentially:

```json
{
  "status": "PUBLISHED",
  "blocks": [
    {
      "uuid": "<your-uuid>",
      "type": "FORM_TITLE",
      "groupUuid": "<your-group-uuid>",
      "groupType": "TEXT",
      "payload": { "title": "Test", "html": "Test" }
    }
  ]
}
```

### UUID handling

Per the docs' note: "Each block requires a unique UUID." Additionally, "You can generate UUIDs using any standard UUID library." No other flags or required fields are specified on this page.

## Response

"The API will respond with a 201 status code" plus form metadata with these fields:

- `id` (e.g., `"m2fK5R"`)
- `name`
- `workspaceId`
- `organizationId`
- `status` (`"PUBLISHED"`)
- `hasDraftBlocks` (`false`)
- `isClosed` (`false`)
- `updatedAt` / `createdAt` (ISO timestamps)

After creation, the form appears in your Tally dashboard containing just the title block.
